operating-hotel-property-due-diligence-b.title: 买下一家在营酒店前，哪些物业问题应先于收益测算核实？
operating-hotel-property-due-diligence-b.titleEn: Buying an Operating Hotel: Which Property Issues Should You Verify Before Modelling Returns?
operating-hotel-property-due-diligence-b.description: 酒店收购物业尽调应先核实权属、用途、消防、改造和空间交付条件，用物业红旗表把核查结果落实到房量、投入、工期和投资决定。
operating-hotel-property-due-diligence-b.descriptionEn: Verify ownership, permitted use, fire safety, alteration feasibility and handover conditions, then connect hotel property due diligence to room inventory, expenditure, timing and the investment decision.
operating-hotel-property-due-diligence-b.author: 迈创兄弟C&T（MarvelBros C&T）
content: 买下一家在营酒店前，应先核实可能改变收购可行性的权属与处分限制、用途、消防与建筑现状，以及买方能否实际控制拟经营的空间，再把这些条件带入收益测算。酒店收购物业尽调，首先要回答的是：买方准备依靠哪些房间、设施和使用权赚钱，这些条件是否有依据。
一家酒店有入住、有收入，能够说明它正在经营，却不能单独证明买方设想的经营规模、改造方案和交割安排都能实现。如果测算中的客房包含尚未核实用途的空间，或者收入提升依赖未经专业评估的改造，即使模型很精细，也可能把不确定条件藏在确定数字里。
这并不要求等所有尽调结束才做初步估算。估算可以与核查并行，但哪些条件已证实、哪些只是设想，必须分别标明。尤其在提交有约束力的报价、支付可能承担违约责任的保证金之前，不能把关键缺口留给“成交以后再说”。
## 先确认买方到底能取得什么
同一个酒店名称，可能对应物业持有人、经营公司和品牌管理方。购买物业、收购持有物业的公司股权、承接租赁经营权，取得的权利和需要核实的责任不同。本文主要讨论境内在营酒店的物业收购核查，股权收购中的物业也可参照核查，但不能照搬资产过户或许可变更的结论。
投资负责人应先把拟交易范围落实到楼栋、楼层、产权单元及附属空间，再由法务核对出售主体与相关权利。销售介绍里的停车场、屋顶设备区、员工宿舍或餐饮空间，不能因为长期由酒店使用，就自动计入买方将来可以持续使用的范围。
权属证书之外，还要查看与交易时点相匹配的登记信息，以及支持实际使用的合同和其他文件。登记状态、合同权利和现场占用各回答一部分问题，不能互相代替。
按经修正的《不动产登记资料查询暂行办法》，有购买意向但尚不能提供相应利害关系证明材料的人，可依规定申请查询部分登记信息，包括不动产自然状况、共有情形及有关权利登记、限制处分情况。查询权限有边界，不能把意向买方能够查询部分信息，写成可以调取全部原始档案。
发现抵押或其他权利负担，也不能仅凭这一项就判定酒店无法交易。应由项目法律团队结合现状、文件和拟定交易安排，核实对处分、交割及交割后使用的具体影响。对投资负责人而言，重要的是哪些条件必须实现、何时实现、由谁提供证据，而不是在表格里简单勾选“有抵押”。
## 酒店收购物业尽调，要把经营规模核实到空间
卖方提供的可售房数，是收入测算的重要输入，却不是物业合法可用范围的完整证明。应把登记和规划用途资料、相关审批及竣工资料、现状平面图，与现场实际功能逐处对照。
重点核查会改变经营假设的差异：客房是否使用了资料中标示为其他功能的区域；餐饮和会议设施是否位于交易范围之外；增建、隔分或改造后的面积是否有相应依据；拟保留的经营功能与买方计划是否一致。发现差异后，先明确需要哪些原件、专业意见或主管部门核实，不凭一张旧图就认定现状违法，也不凭经营多年就认定无需处理。
投资测算至少要能说明，房间数量、可经营面积和配套能力分别依据哪份资料。尚未核实的新增空间，可以作为待验证方案单独测算；在形成投资决定时，不能把它与已经确认的经营能力混在一起。
## 消防资料要对应当前布局和经营场所
消防核查容易被简化成“有没有消防证”。对在营酒店，应分别核查建设工程消防设计审查、验收或备案抽查资料，以及公众聚集场所投入使用、营业前消防安全检查的相关手续，并核对它们对应的地址、范围和实际状态。
住建部《建设工程消防设计审查验收管理暂行规定》区分特殊建设工程的审查验收与其他建设工程的备案抽查；《消防法》第十五条另行规定公众聚集场所营业前的消防安全检查。两类事项有不同作用，不能拿其中一份材料概括全部消防条件。
买方真正需要追问的是：当年材料覆盖哪些区域，后来是否改过客房布局、疏散路线或使用功能，现有图纸与现场是否一致，是否存在尚未处理完的检查意见。是否涉及补办、重新申请或改造，应结合工程历史、现状和拟实施方案，由相应专业人员核实。
对老建筑，也不能直接用今天的新要求倒推过去的手续一律无效，或者反过来认为旧手续可以覆盖今后所有改造。资料审查与现场核查应衔接，历史批准范围和此次拟改变的部分要分开说明。
## 改造能否实现，先于改造能赚多少
如果投资回报依赖增加客房、调整餐饮或重做公共区域，就应先让工程和设计人员确认这些改变是否有实现条件。
《建筑法》第四十九条对涉及建筑主体和承重结构变动的装修，要求施工前由原设计单位或具有相应资质条件的设计单位提出设计方案。这意味着，涉及结构的经营设想不能只凭装修报价确定可行性。
结构条件、设备容量、检修空间以及共有设施的使用安排，都可能改变改造范围、成本和工期。工程人员需要说明发现了什么、还需什么检查、能否形成可实施方案，以及估算中有哪些未确定事项。财务再据此调整投入、可售房量、停业影响和恢复经营的时间，而不是先填一个改造费总数，再要求工程把方案塞进去。
供能问题可继续使用《酒店投资尽调：水、电、燃气供应要查清哪些问题？》中的专项方法。本篇不重复设备清单，重点是把专业核查结果送回投资假设。
## 使用中的空间，不一定能按计划交付
物业核查还应覆盖租赁、第三方占用和共有设施。即使交易范围已经写清，买方仍需知道哪些区域由谁使用、依据是什么、拟定交割安排能否落实。
例如，计划自营的餐饮区如果正在由第三方使用，就应取得适用合同及补充文件，核对使用范围和项目法律团队对交付条件的意见。不能只听卖方口头承诺“到时可以收回”。如果经营依赖共用出入口、停车、供配电或设备机房，还要确认使用和维护安排。
这些条件对测算的影响，应具体落到能否按时开放、是否需要替代空间、是否增加投入或经常性支出。合同解除、权利承接和许可变更不能用统一答案处理，需要结合本项目交易方式核实。
## 把物业红旗表写成投资决定的依据
“红旗”是需要进一步处理的重要信号，不等于已经认定违法或必须放弃交易。投资负责人可以用一张表，把每一项关键物业假设写成一行。
每行依次记录：拟依赖的经营条件，核查对象及空间范围，已取得的文件与日期，尚缺的原件或专业核验，可能影响的房量、投入或工期，当前处理决定，责任人，补证时点，以及关闭该事项所需的证据。
处理决定分三类。对可能使拟定用途或交割无法实现、且尚无可靠解决路径的事项，暂停依赖该条件作出不可逆承诺；对可以核实但资料尚不充分的事项，限定补证时间和下一决策节点；对已有可实施处理方案的事项，把有依据的费用、工期和限制纳入报价及资本开支。未完成法律或工程核验的事项，不能仅以卖方答复作为结案依据。
公开交易条款也能帮助买方确定核查应在什么时间完成。北京市公共资源交易服务平台2026年9月8日披露的中青旅山水酒店集团股份及相关债权项目，将公告期设为尽职调查期，并把通过资格确认、交纳保证金与认可披露及备查文件的承诺相联系。这里只引用该次挂牌条件，不代表其今日交易状态，也不是单体物业买卖的通用条款。
买方从这条公开线索应落实的动作，是在承担相关承诺前安排原件查阅和专业核验，并确认自己的资料与时间是否足够。本文未取得该项目备查全文，不评价其具体物业状况或交易风险。卖方怎样组织这些材料，可参阅《酒店准备出售，先整理哪一份买方能复核的数据室？》；买方还要判断材料是否支持自己的经营假设。
## 先用一个关键假设检验这张表
以下为方法示例，并非真实项目：买方计划把一处会议区域改为客房，收益模型已经计入新增房量，但现有材料尚不能说明用途、消防和结构条件是否支持改造。
这条记录的当前结论应是“新增房量尚待证实”。由投资负责人协调法务、工程和设计人员核对相关资料及现场，列明可能需要的批准、设计、施工和停业安排。财务分别测算维持现状与改造实现的情景，不把未经证实的新增收入直接放入确定回报。
如果核实后可以实施，再依据方案更新费用和时间；如果只能减少新增房量，或停业时间使投资条件不再成立，就调整报价、修改方案或停止推进。填完一行不是结果，经营假设得到证实、修正或撤回，才是这次核查的价值。
第一次投资评审前，可先选一个最影响收益、又最容易查证的物业条件走完上述过程，再扩展到全部重大事项。业主或投委会负责确定可接受的投资条件并授权查阅和专业核验；投资负责人组织核查，专业团队对各自领域提出意见，财务负责模型对应。交割前还应按项目安排更新可能变化的权利和占用状态。
资料齐全、用途明确且不依赖重大改造的项目，可以让物业核查与财务研究同步推进；产权复杂、历史改造较多或依赖改变用途的项目，则应更早投入专业核验。文章提供的是投资判断的组织方法，不能替代具体项目的法律意见、工程鉴定或审批结论。

contentEn: Before buying an operating hotel, verify the ownership and restrictions on disposal, permitted use, fire safety and building conditions, and whether the buyer can actually control the spaces it intends to operate. Establish the conditions that could change the acquisition's feasibility, then incorporate them into the return model. Hotel property due diligence begins with a question: which rooms, facilities and rights of use will generate the expected income, and what evidence supports those assumptions?

Guests and revenue demonstrate that a hotel is trading. They do not, by themselves, establish that the buyer's intended operating scale, refurbishment plan and completion arrangements are achievable. If projected room inventory includes space whose permitted use has not been verified, or revenue growth depends on alterations not yet assessed by professionals, even a detailed model may conceal uncertain conditions within apparently definite figures.

This does not mean waiting until all due diligence is complete before making an initial estimate. Modelling and verification can proceed together, provided confirmed conditions are distinguished from assumptions. In particular, before submitting a binding offer or paying a deposit that could carry liability for breach, do not leave critical gaps to be resolved after the transaction.
## Establish what the buyer will acquire

A single hotel name may encompass a property owner, an operating company and a brand manager. Purchasing the property, acquiring shares in a property-holding company and taking over leasehold operating rights confer different rights and require different responsibilities to be checked. This article primarily addresses property acquisition checks for operating hotels in mainland China. The property element of a share acquisition can be examined along similar lines, but conclusions about asset transfers or changes to permits cannot simply be carried across.

The investment lead should first define the proposed transaction in terms of buildings, floors, registered property units and ancillary spaces. Legal advisers should then verify the selling entity and the relevant rights. Parking areas, rooftop plant space, staff accommodation or dining areas described in sales materials should not automatically be included in the buyer's future usable space merely because the hotel has used them for years.

Alongside ownership certificates, examine registration information relevant to the transaction date, as well as contracts and other documents supporting actual use. Registration status, contractual rights and physical occupation answer different parts of the question; none substitutes for the others.

Under the amended Interim Measures for Enquiries into Real Estate Registration Materials, a prospective purchaser who cannot yet supply the relevant evidence of an interest may apply, as prescribed, to inspect certain registration information. This includes the property's physical particulars, co-ownership and relevant registered rights and restrictions on disposal. Access is limited: the right to inspect some information does not mean an intending buyer can obtain the entire underlying file.

The presence of a mortgage or another encumbrance does not, on its own, establish that the hotel cannot be transacted. The project's legal team should assess the implications for disposal, completion and subsequent use against the current circumstances, documents and proposed transaction arrangements. The investment lead needs to know which conditions must be met, when and with what evidence, rather than simply ticking a box marked “mortgaged”.
## Hotel property due diligence must link operating capacity to specific spaces

The seller's available room count is an important revenue-model input. It is not complete evidence of the property's lawful usable extent. Compare registration and planning-use records, relevant approvals and completion documents, and current floor plans with the actual function of each space.

Focus on differences that could change the operating assumptions. Are guestrooms located in areas shown in the records as serving another function? Are dining or meeting facilities outside the transaction boundary? Is there supporting documentation for space added, subdivided or altered? Do the functions to be retained match the buyer's plan? When differences emerge, establish which originals, professional opinions or checks with the competent authorities are needed. An old drawing alone does not prove that the current arrangement is unlawful, and years of trading do not prove that no action is required.

The investment model should identify the documents supporting room numbers, operating floor area and ancillary capacity. Unverified additional space can be modelled separately as an option to test. When making an investment decision, it should not be combined with established operating capacity as though both were equally certain.
## Match fire safety records to the current layout and premises

Fire safety review is easily reduced to asking whether there is a “fire certificate”. For an operating hotel, separately examine the construction project's fire safety design review, acceptance or filing and spot-check records, and the relevant procedures for fire safety inspection before a public gathering venue enters use or opens for business. Check the address, scope and actual condition to which each relates.

The Ministry of Housing and Urban-Rural Development's Interim Provisions on the Administration of Fire Safety Design Review and Acceptance of Construction Projects distinguish review and acceptance for special construction projects from filing and spot checks for other projects. Article 15 of the Fire Protection Law separately addresses fire safety inspections before public gathering venues open for business. These procedures serve different purposes; one document cannot stand for all fire safety conditions.

The buyer needs to establish which areas the original documents covered, whether guestroom layouts, escape routes or functions subsequently changed, whether current drawings match the site, and whether inspection findings remain unresolved. Any need to complete missing procedures, reapply or alter the premises should be assessed by the relevant professionals against the project's history, current condition and proposed work.

For older buildings, current requirements should not simply be applied retrospectively to declare all past procedures invalid. Equally, old approvals should not be assumed to cover every future alteration. Document review and site inspection need to connect, with the historically approved scope distinguished from the changes now proposed.
## Establish whether alterations are feasible before estimating their return
If the return depends on adding rooms, changing dining facilities or remodelling public areas, engineering and design professionals should first establish whether those changes are feasible.

Article 49 of the Construction Law requires a design proposal from the original design organisation or an appropriately qualified design organisation before renovation work that alters the building's main structure or load-bearing structure. An operating proposal involving structural alterations therefore cannot be judged feasible solely from a refurbishment quotation.

Structural conditions, equipment capacity, maintenance access and arrangements for shared facilities may change the scope, cost and duration of the work. Engineering advisers need to explain what they have found, what further checks are needed, whether an implementable scheme can be developed and what remains uncertain in the estimates. Finance can then adjust capital expenditure, available room inventory, closure effects and the reopening timetable. The sequence should not begin with a fixed refurbishment allowance that engineering is expected to accommodate.

The specialist approach in “Water, Power and Gas Supply: Due Diligence for Hotel Investors” can be used for utility questions. This article does not repeat the equipment checklist; its purpose is to bring professional findings back into the investment assumptions.
## Space in use may not be available for handover as planned

Property review should also cover leases, third-party occupation and shared facilities. Even where the transaction boundary is clear, the buyer needs to know who uses each area, on what basis, and whether the proposed completion arrangements can be implemented.

For example, if a dining area intended for in-house operation is occupied by a third party, obtain the applicable contract and supplementary documents. Check the occupied area and the legal team's advice on the conditions for handover. Do not rely solely on a seller's verbal assurance that the space can be recovered when needed. If operations depend on shared entrances, parking, power distribution or plant rooms, confirm the arrangements for use and maintenance.

Translate these findings into specific model implications: whether facilities can open on time, whether substitute space is needed, and whether capital or recurring expenditure increases. Contract termination, succession to rights and changes to permits cannot be answered uniformly; they require assessment against the particular transaction structure.
## Make the property red-flag register support an investment decision

A red flag is a significant issue requiring attention. It does not necessarily mean that a breach has been established or that the transaction must be abandoned. The investment lead can use one register, with a separate row for each material property assumption.

Each row should record the operating condition being relied on, the asset and spatial scope being checked, documents obtained and their dates, missing originals or professional verification, possible effects on room inventory, expenditure or timing, the current response, the responsible person, the deadline for further evidence, and the evidence required to close the issue.

Responses fall into three categories. Where an issue could prevent the proposed use or completion and no reliable solution has been established, pause irreversible commitments that depend on that condition. Where the issue can be verified but information is incomplete, set a deadline for evidence and identify the next decision point. Where an implementable remedy is supported, incorporate substantiated cost, timing and restrictions into the offer and capital expenditure plan. A seller's response alone should not close an issue still awaiting legal or engineering verification.

Public transaction terms can also help a buyer establish when checks need to be completed. A September 8, 2026 disclosure on the Beijing Public Resources Trading Service Platform concerning shares in CYTS Shanshui Hotel Group and related receivables designated the announcement period for due diligence. It linked qualification confirmation and payment of the deposit with commitments recognising the disclosed documents and materials available for inspection. This is a reference to that listing's conditions, not its transaction status today or a universal rule for individual property sales.

The buyer's practical response is to arrange access to originals and professional verification before making the relevant commitments, and to establish whether the available information and time are sufficient. This article has not obtained the complete inspection files for that project and does not assess its property condition or transaction risks. “Preparing to Sell a Hotel: Which Data Room Should the Seller Organise First?” explains how a seller can organise the materials. The buyer must also decide whether they support its own operating assumptions.
## Test the register with one important assumption

The following is a methodological illustration, not a real project. A buyer plans to convert a meeting area into guestrooms, and the return model already includes the additional rooms. The available documents do not yet establish whether permitted use, fire safety and structural conditions support the conversion.

The current conclusion for this entry should be “additional room inventory remains unverified”. The investment lead should coordinate legal, engineering and design specialists to examine the records and site, identifying potential approval, design, construction and closure requirements. Finance should model the existing configuration and successful conversion separately, without treating unverified additional revenue as a certain return.

If verification supports the scheme, update cost and timing from the proposed design. If fewer additional rooms are feasible, or the closure period undermines the investment case, adjust the offer, revise the scheme or stop proceeding. Completing a row is not the result. The value of the review lies in an operating assumption being substantiated, revised or withdrawn.

Before the first investment review, select one property condition that materially affects returns and can be checked readily. Work through that condition, then extend the process to all material issues. The owner or investment committee should define acceptable investment conditions and authorise access and professional verification. The investment lead organises the review, specialists provide opinions within their respective fields, and finance reconciles the findings with the model. Before completion, update potentially changing rights and occupation information in line with the project's arrangements.

Projects with complete records, clear use and no reliance on major alterations can run property checks alongside financial analysis. Those with complex ownership, extensive historical alterations or dependence on a change of use need professional verification earlier. This article provides a way to organise investment judgment; it does not replace project-specific legal advice, engineering assessments or regulatory decisions.
